x: O'Connor, Poly H., forced the pace at the start with Weatherill and Stansbury, both of South London H., in close attendance Footer, who had for a mile been well in the rear, then came through with a rush and the leaders commenced to draw away from the rest of the field.
Suddenly the leaders appear again; Oddie, Tomlin, Weatherill and Broadley......S.L.H. have three in seven......there is a gap......Harry Payne 9th......What about Belgrave?

In the Senior race we had great hopes of seeing Arthur Allum head the field, but at the half-distance it was apparent that he had undergone a "bad time" in the early stages, for he was in the fifth position, about 200 yards behind the leader, Weatherill, of South London Harriers.

Carter being up in the front, with Weatherill and Tebbutt of S.L.H. At the first lap Weatherill was "out on his own" and, politely inquiring how far he was in front, seemed to draw further ahead; but it was very gratifying to see a "Claret and Gold" in second place, carried by Carter, with Tebbutt at his shoulder.
Weatherill, of S.L.H., and hereafter everyone had a good view of Weatherill's back. Bert Footer ran what must have been the best and also pluckiest race of his career.
"Up Weatherill" an "Irrepressible" shouted. Yes, there was Weatherill and—oh, cheers! there was "our Bert" also, bunched between 28 and the thirties.
Penny was in the lead with Weatherill, the South London Harrier, and our hopes were soon raised when we saw Footer lying 6th, followed by Carter 8th, and Abberton 10th.
It was particularly interesting to note that Weatherill scored as England's sixth man, and so the South supplied three of the six scoring men, the Midlands one, and the North two.
At four miles Penny and Weatherill (S.L.H.) led the field. Allum was 5th, Flower 14th, Carter 15th, Footer 30th, closely followed by Rice, Walker and Shaw in a bunch, and Taylor about 50th.

At four miles Burns (Elswick) was in the lead, followed by Sutherland (Birchfield), Holden (Tipton), Eaton (Salford), Dodd (Wirral), Robinson (Birchfield), Penny (Belgrave) and Weatherill (S.L.H.) Birchfield were said to have six men in 19 at this point, and we looked certain of a place.
After a mile, however, Harwood, of Surrey A.C., who had just returned from abroad after a spell in the Army, had a lead of about 40 yards with Weatherill, of S.L.H., and myself next.
The rest of the field passed me strung out, excepting Weatherill and Jones, who had gone by at the tail of the centre bunch, and looked safe enough.

In spite of this brilliant piece of running, his time was beaten by Weatherill, of S.L.H., who got within a second of stage record, and in doing so took his club into fourth place, which they retained to the end.

Then came Hines, Weatherill, Penny fifth, Carter sixth, Cohen seventh, Ring thirteenth, and Wood seventeenth. This scoring enabled us to win comfortably from Surrey A.C., thus making our tenth win in the last twelve years.

Trevor Hart hands over to Charlie Walker with Weatherill (Portsmouth) waiting to take over from the fast-finishing Tulloh. Hugh Barrow will certainly not forget his first road relay in Belgrave colours.
